summary: Heiner Eichner was a scholar in linguistics and Indology. He studied at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg (~1964–1974) under Karl Hoffmann (~1965–1974) and later held a post at the University of Vienna (~1989–2010).
Heinrich August Eduard Schaeffer was an Indologist and religious studies scholar who studied at the University of Leipzig. He served as principal at the Evangelical Lutheran Central High School.

Heinrich August Jäschke was a scholar of Tibetology and linguistics. He studied at Pädagogium Niesky and Gnadenfeld Theological Seminary, later serving as co-director at Pädagogium Niesky (1842–1856) and as a Moravian missionary in Kyelang (1856–1863).

Heinrich Blatt was a scholar of Indology and linguistics. He studied at the universities of Munich, Leipzig, Berlin, Würzburg, and Erlangen-Nuremberg, earning a Ph.D. at the latter (~1920–1923), and worked as a librarian at Würzburg University Library (1923–1946).

Heinrich Blochmann worked in Iranian and Central Asian studies, Indology, and history and archaeology. He studied under Fleischer at Leipzig, Hase at Paris, and at the University of Calcutta, later serving as principal of Aliah University and secretary of The Asiatic Society.
Heinrich Brunn was a scholar in history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Bonn (~1839–1843) and held a post at the University of Munich (~1865–1894).

Heinrich Düntzer worked in linguistics and Indology. He studied at the University of Bonn and under Franz Bopp in Berlin. He held positions at the University of Bonn (~1836–1846) and as librarian at the Dreikönigsgymnasium (1846–1885).

Heinrich Ewald was a scholar in linguistics, Indology, and religious studies. He studied at the University of Göttingen under Thomas Christian Tychsen, and held professorships at Göttingen (1824–1837, 1848–1867) and the University of Tübingen (1838–1848).

Heinrich Franz Joseph Junker was a scholar of Iranian and Central Asian studies and linguistics. After earning his Ph.D. under Christian Bartholomae at Heidelberg, he held professorships at the universities of Hamburg, Leipzig (1926–1945), and Humboldt University of Berlin (1951).
Heinrich Gustav Hotho was a scholar in philosophy. He studied at Humboldt University of Berlin (~1820–1826) and subsequently held an academic post there (~1829–1873).
Heinrich Gössel was an Indologist. He earned his Ph.D. at the University of Leipzig (~1908–1913) studying under Ernst Windisch, and later served as an assistant there in 1917.

Heinrich Hackmann worked in Sinology, religious studies, and Buddhist studies. He studied at the universities of Leipzig, Göttingen, and Basel, and served as privatdozent at Göttingen (~1893–1894) and professor of the history of religions at the University of Amsterdam (1913–1934).

Heinrich Hettrich was a scholar in linguistics, Indology, and Iranian and Central Asian studies. He studied at Saarland, Giessen, and Munich, and held the chair of comparative linguistics at the University of Würzburg starting in 1989.

Heinrich Hübschmann worked in linguistics, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and Indology. He studied at Jena, Tübingen, Munich (Ph.D. under Martin Haug), and Leipzig, later holding a professorship in comparative linguistics at the University of Strasbourg from 1877.

Heinrich Kiepert was a scholar of history and archaeology. He studied at Berlin and Jena, and later served as cartographic director at Geographisches Institut Weimar and Dietrich Reimer Verlag, and as professor of geography at Humboldt University of Berlin.

Heinrich Leberecht Fleischer was a scholar in linguistics. He studied at the University of Leipzig and under Silvestre de Sacy, Caussin de Perceval, Chézy, and Jaubert in Paris, later holding the chair of oriental languages at Leipzig from 1836.

Heinrich Lüders was an Indologist and linguist who studied at Göttingen under Franz Kielhorn. He held the chair of ancient Indian language and literature at Humboldt University of Berlin (1909–1935) and served as secretary of the Prussian Academy of Sciences (1920–1938).

Heinrich Meinhard was an Indologist and archaeologist who earned his Ph.D. at Bonn under Willibald Kirfel. He worked at the Ethnological Museum of Berlin, Pitt Rivers Museum, and became Reader of Anthropology at Durham University in 1950.

Heinrich Meyer-Benfey was an Indologist who studied at the University of Göttingen (~1888–1895). He later served as privatdozent (1919) and associate professor of German (1923–1938) at the University of Hamburg.

Heinrich Nau was an Indologist. He studied at the University of Marburg, Concordia Seminary, and Martin Luther University of Halle-Wittenberg, where he completed his Ph.D. under Eugen Hultzsch (~1918–1920).
